notes.b: Cheese is made by coagulating (setting) milk protein and draining off the liquid whey. Cheeses are grouped by how firm and moist they are and by how they are ripened, so each class has typical examples that exams ask you to name.
points: Hard cheese is low in moisture, firm and matured for longer, so it keeps well. Examples are Cheddar, Parmesan, Cheshire and Emmenthal.
Semi-hard or semi-soft cheese sits between hard and soft in firmness. Examples are Gouda, Edam and Halloumi.

Soft cheese is high in moisture. Cottage cheese, cream cheese, feta and mozzarella are fresh (eaten young, with feta also kept in brine), while Brie and Camembert are ripened by a mould on the surface.
Blue-veined cheese is ripened by a mould that grows through the cheese, giving the blue veins. Examples are Cashel Blue (an Irish cheese), Stilton, Roquefort and Gorgonzola.

Processed cheese is natural cheese melted and blended with emulsifying salts and other ingredients, then moulded into a uniform product, so it has a longer shelf life and melts easily. Examples are cheese slices, cheese spreads and processed cheddars.
Smoked cheese is cheese flavoured by smoking, often sold as a processed product, so it is grouped with processed cheese.
Diagram: draw a table with the columns class, description, examples and uses, with one row for each class of cheese.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to classify cheese and give an example in each class. Use Edam, Gouda or Halloumi for semi-hard and Cashel Blue, Roquefort or Gorgonzola for blue, and file smoked cheese with processed cheese.

notes.b: Cheese is concentrated milk: most of the water and lactose are drained away, leaving the protein, fat and minerals. That is why it is rich in some nutrients and has none of others.
points: Protein is about 10 to 27% of cheese, mostly casein. It is high biological value (HBV) protein, containing all the essential amino acids (the ones the body cannot make), for growth, repair and the making of enzymes, hormones and antibodies.
Protein content varies by type, because soft cheese contains less protein than hard cheese.
Fat is about 4 to 35%, mostly saturated, with cholesterol, so full-fat cheese supplies concentrated energy. Cottage cheese is about 4% fat.
The more water in a cheese, the less fat it has, and cheese made from skimmed milk is lower in fat.
Carbohydrate is 0 to about 1.5%, because most of the lactose drains away in the whey and the rest changes to lactic acid.
Vitamin A and beta-carotene support healthy skin, vision and membranes. Riboflavin (B2) and B12 are the main B group vitamins supplied.
Calcium and phosphorus support bones and teeth, and some vitamin D is supplied to help calcium absorption. Total minerals are about 1.5 to 4%.
Sodium comes mainly from the salt added during production, so cheddar and processed cheese are high in salt. Cheese is deficient in vitamin C, iron and fibre, and its water content varies by type.
notes.tip: Nutritive value questions expect HBV protein, saturated fat, no carbohydrate, calcium, and vitamins A, D and B2 and sodium. Remember what cheese lacks: vitamin C, iron and fibre.

notes.b: Dietetic value means how suitable cheese is for different people and diets. It has strong points as a food and some limits that matter for health.
points: Cheese is a relatively cheap protein food with no waste, needs no cooking, and suits packed lunches and snacks.
Protein and calcium support growth in children and adolescents, and are needed in pregnancy and by nursing mothers.
Cheese is a high-energy food because of its fat, so it suits active people.

Cottage cheese and low-fat varieties suit low-kilocalorie, low-cholesterol and weight-watching diets. Full-fat cheeses are high in saturated fat and salt, so people with heart disease or high blood pressure should limit them.
Some cheeses are difficult to digest because they are high in fat.

Pregnant women are advised to avoid mould-ripened soft cheeses such as Brie and Camembert, blue cheeses and soft cheeses made from unpasteurised milk, because of the risk of listeria (a food poisoning bacterium). Hard cheese, cottage cheese, cream cheese and pasteurised processed cheese are considered safe.
Cheese lacks carbohydrate and fibre, so it should be eaten with foods such as bread, crackers, pasta or potatoes, and with vegetables or fruit for fibre and vitamin C.

Cheese is versatile and comes in wide variety, which helps variety in the diet. It sits on the milk, yoghurt and cheese shelf of the Food Pyramid, where it should be eaten in small amounts and in lower-fat forms.
notes.tip: Exams ask for dietetic points such as versatile, cheap and no waste, and for who should limit cheese. When you say pregnant women avoid cheese, name the mould-ripened, blue and unpasteurised types, because safe soft cheeses exist, such as cottage and cream cheese.

notes.b: Two ingredients turn liquid milk into cheese: bacteria that sour it, and an enzyme that sets it. Each does a different job, and exams often ask you to keep them apart.
points: Lactic acid bacteria are added to pasteurised milk as a starter culture. They convert lactose (milk sugar) into lactic acid, which preserves the cheese, adds flavour and helps the curd to form.

Rennet contains the enzyme rennin, which changes caseinogen (the soluble milk protein) into casein (the insoluble form). Rennet traditionally comes from calf stomach, while vegetarian rennet is made from microbes or plants.
The casein coagulates, so the milk proteins bond and set, and the milk separates into curds and whey.
Curds are the solid part. Whey is the liquid part, which holds most of the lactose and water, so little lactose stays in the cheese.
notes.tip: Lactic acid is made by the bacteria, not by the rennet, and rennin (rennet) is the enzyme. Short questions ask the role of each, or a fill-in on lactic acid, rennin and curds.

notes.b: Making cheese follows a fixed order, from adding the bacteria to ripening. Learn the stages in sequence, with what each one achieves.
points: 1. A culture of lactic acid bacteria is added to pasteurised milk, to turn lactose into lactic acid.
2. The milk is heated to about 30°C and rennet is added. Left to stand for about 30 minutes, it separates into curds and whey.
3. The curds are cut or chopped to release more whey, and the whey is drained off.
4. The curds are heated to 35 to 40°C (called scalding), which squeezes out more whey and gives the correct consistency.
5. Cheddaring (for Cheddar and similar cheeses): the curds are cut into blocks and piled on each other, and turned, to complete drainage of the whey.
6. The blocks are milled (cut) and about 2% salt is added for flavour and preservation.
7. The salted curds are placed in moulds and pressed. The moulds may be sprayed with hot water so that a protective rind forms.

8. The cheese is removed from the moulds, date stamped, and stored for about 3 to 12 months to ripen (mature), then graded. Ripening develops flavour and texture, and longer maturing gives a stronger, drier cheese.
notes.tip: The production question is marked in points worth two marks each: about seven stages in order, plus one packaging and one labelling point. Include lactic acid bacteria and what they do, rennet and what it does, curds and whey, chopping and draining, scalding, cheddaring, salting, moulding and pressing, and ripening and grading. Diagram: a flow chart of the stages.

notes.h: How blue and soft ripened cheeses differ
notes.b: The steps above give a hard cheese such as Cheddar. Ripened cheeses use a mould to get their character, which is the contrast to know.
points: Blue cheese has a mould added, and the cheese is pierced to let air in, so the mould can grow through it.
Soft ripened cheeses such as Brie and Camembert have a mould growing on the surface.

notes.b: Packaging protects the cheese, and labelling tells the buyer what it is and how to store it. Both carry marks in the production question.
points: Cheese is vacuum packed in polythene (plastic) zip-lock bags, which extends shelf life. The pack protects it from mould and drying.
Waxed paper or wax coating and plastic tubs are used, with tubs suiting smaller portions.
The label gives the type of cheese, brand, quantity and nutritional information.
The label also gives the date stamp, storage instructions and allergen information (milk).
Labels must comply with Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.

notes.b: Heat changes both the protein and the fat in cheese. Knowing these changes explains how to cook it well.
points: Colour changes as the cheese browns.
The protein coagulates and shrinks.
The fat melts, and if the cheese is overheated the fat separates from it and makes it oily.
Overcooked cheese becomes stringy, tough and hard to digest, and overcooking can carbonise (burn) it.
Little loss of nutrients occurs when cheese is cooked.
To avoid these faults, grate or slice the cheese, cook it at a moderate temperature for a short time, and add it at the end of a sauce.
notes.tip: Effects of heat on cheese is asked as a list. Give browning, protein coagulating and shrinking, fat melting and separating, stringy and tough when overcooked, and little nutrient loss.

notes.b: Cheese is versatile because it can be eaten cold, melted, grated or cooked into dishes. Match the type of cheese to the dish.
points: Sandwiches and snacks, including cheese slices in sandwiches.
Baking and pastry, such as cheese scones, cheese pastry and cheese straws.
Savoury and sweet fillings, and sauces such as white cheese sauce and macaroni cheese.
Desserts, such as cheesecake made with cream cheese, and cheeseboards.
Main ingredient in pizza, pasta, potato and salad dishes.
Dips, fondue, and toppings and garnishes such as gratin.

Choosing the cheese: Parmesan, a hard cheese, is grated over pasta carbonara; cream cheese is used in lemon cheesecake; cheddar slices are used in a cheese sandwich; mozzarella goes on pizza; grated hard cheese suits toppings that brown.
notes.tip: When asked to choose a cheese for a dish, name the cheese and say why it suits, as in cream cheese for a cheesecake. Culinary uses questions ask for three uses.

notes.b: Irish farmhouse cheese is a speciality (artisan) food that has grown in popularity. Exams ask for reasons, each explained.
points: Farmhouse cheese is made on the farm in small quantities, mainly by hand, usually from the farm's own cow's, goat's or sheep's milk.
Examples are Cashel Blue (Co Tipperary, blue), Gubbeen (West Cork, washed rind), Durrus (West Cork) and Coolea (Co Cork, Gouda style).
Its distinctive flavours, textures and degrees of maturity differ from mass-produced cheese, and there is a wide variety, including soft, hard, blue, flavoured, organic and reduced-fat cheeses.
It is seen as high quality, hygienic, less processed and more natural.
Consumers value traceable local food, with fewer food miles, and support for local employment and rural family farm businesses.
It is promoted and sold at farmers' markets, specialist shops, restaurants, food tourism, and by celebrity chefs and the media, and it suits the cheeseboard and entertaining.
Awards and quality assurance strengthen its premium image.
notes.tip: Give three reasons for the popularity of Irish cheese made on small farms and explain each, for example fewer food miles because it is local, or a premium image because of awards.

keyTerms.definition: Lactic acid bacteria added to milk at the start of cheese making, which convert lactose into lactic acid.
A preparation containing the enzyme rennin, which coagulates caseinogen into casein during cheese making.
The milk protein that coagulates to form the solid structure of cheese curds.
The solid part of milk that forms when casein coagulates, which is pressed into cheese.
The liquid part of milk that separates from curds, containing most of the lactose.
The stage in cheese making where curds are cut into blocks and piled together to drain away whey.
Heating curds to 35 to 40°C to squeeze out more whey and achieve the correct consistency.
Cheese blended and heated with other ingredients to give a uniform product, such as cheese slices or spreads.
A cheese ripened by a mould that grows through the body of the cheese, giving blue veins.
Cheese made on a farm in small batches, with distinctive flavour and character.

questions.prompt: Outline how curds and whey are separated when making a hard cheese.
questions.model: A lactic acid culture is added to pasteurised milk, and the milk is heated to about 30°C. Rennet is added; its enzyme changes caseinogen into casein, which coagulates the milk. The mixture separates into curds and whey. The curds are chopped to release more whey, which is drained off, and the curds are then heated and pressed.

questions.prompt: Discuss the nutritional significance of full-fat and reduced-fat cheese, and explain how cheese should be combined with other foods to give a balanced meal.
questions.model: Nutritional significance: HBV protein for growth and repair; calcium and phosphorus for bones and teeth; vitamins A and B2, with B12 and some vitamin D; full-fat cheese high in saturated fat, cholesterol and energy; reduced-fat cheese lower in fat and energy, suiting low-cholesterol and weight-watching diets; high in salt, especially cheddar; little carbohydrate, and no vitamin C, iron or fibre. Combination: eat with wholegrain bread or other carbohydrate, with vegetables or fruit for fibre and vitamin C, and with iron-rich foods; control portions of full-fat, salty cheese; avoid soft cheeses during pregnancy.
